options.why: Degenerative findings occur in symptomatic and asymptomatic people. An anatomic abnormality is not automatically the cause of symptoms.

options.text: Ignore all MRI findings in every patient
options.why: MRI can be valuable in radiculopathy, CIDP roots, and Hirayama disease when clinically matched.

options.text: Treat all MRI changes with plasma exchange
options.why: Mechanical degeneration does not by itself justify immunotherapy.

options.text: Diagnose MS from any degenerative disc
options.why: Disc degeneration is not a demyelinating plaque.

stem: Why does myelin permit rapid saltatory conduction?

options.text: It forces every internodal membrane segment to fire a full action potential
options.why: That describes continuous rather than saltatory conduction.

options.text: It allows action potentials to travel through blood vessels
options.why: Signals propagate along axons, not vessel lumens.

options.text: It eliminates the need for axonal ion channels
options.why: Nodes still require voltage-gated channels.

options.text: It converts motor axons into muscle fibers
options.why: Myelination does not change cell lineage.

options.text: It limits membrane current leak so depolarization efficiently reaches the next node
options.why: Myelin increases membrane resistance and lowers effective capacitance across internodes. Regenerative action potentials occur at nodes of Ranvier.

stem: How is motor conduction velocity calculated using two stimulation sites?

options.text: Proximal latency alone divided by distal amplitude
options.why: This does not isolate segment conduction time.

options.text: Distance between sites divided by the difference in proximal and distal onset latencies
options.why: Subtracting distal from proximal latency largely removes the shared distal nerve, NMJ, and muscle delay, leaving conduction time for the intervening nerve segment.

options.text: CMAP amplitude divided by serum protein
options.why: These quantities do not measure conduction speed.
Fasciculations are not a velocity measurement.

options.text: Distance from eye to cortex divided by P100 amplitude
options.why: This is unrelated to routine motor NCS velocity.

stem: NCS shows low CMAP and SNAP amplitudes with relatively preserved velocity and distal latency. Which process is favored?

options.text: Pure demyelination with no axonal loss in every case
options.why: Primary demyelination more strongly affects velocity and latency, although amplitude can also fall from block or secondary axonal loss.
Loss of functioning axons reduces response amplitude. Surviving axons can conduct at near-normal speeds; marked nonuniform slowing suggests additional myelin dysfunction.
Peripheral motor and sensory response abnormalities do not localize to the optic nerve.
Low amplitudes are abnormal when technical and physiologic factors are excluded.
Lens opacity does not reduce peripheral CMAPs or SNAPs.

stem: NCS shows prolonged distal motor latencies, marked conduction slowing, and temporal dispersion across multiple nerves. Which process is favored?

options.text: Pure muscle disease as the only explanation
options.why: Myopathy does not generally cause this widespread demyelinating nerve pattern.
CNS lesions do not generally cause diffuse peripheral demyelinating NCS changes.
These are abnormal findings.
Cataract does not affect limb nerve conduction.

Marked slowing and dispersion support myelin dysfunction when thresholds, temperature, amplitudes, and entrapment confounders are considered. Clinical context determines whether CIDP or another disorder is present.

stem: Proximal stimulation produces a much smaller CMAP than distal stimulation across a non-entrapment segment. What does this suggest?

options.why: Retinal vascular changes do not explain a segmental motor block.
This is a motor nerve conduction finding.
Conduction block instead raises concern for treatable motor or demyelinating neuropathies.

options.text: Increased motor unit recruitment by definition
options.why: Recruitment is assessed with voluntary needle EMG, not this response comparison.
Some axons fail to conduct through the intervening segment. Block supports acquired nerve dysfunction, but technical factors and nodal axonal GBS variants must also be considered.

stem: What should a healthy relaxed muscle usually show after insertional activity has settled?

options.why: Fibrillations suggest denervation or some myopathies rather than normal resting activity.

options.text: Giant voluntarily activated motor units without effort
options.why: Motor unit activation requires contraction; giant units can reflect chronic reinnervation.

options.text: A maximal interference pattern at rest
options.why: An interference pattern occurs with voluntary recruitment.
Persistent fibrillations or positive sharp waves are abnormal spontaneous single-fiber activity. Interpretation must consider insertion, endplate activity, and sampling.
P100 belongs to visual evoked potentials.

stem: Needle EMG shows fibrillations and positive sharp waves. Which interpretation is best?

options.text: Active muscle fiber instability, often from denervation or myopathy
options.why: These are spontaneous single-fiber discharges. They are not specific to ALS and must be interpreted with distribution and other findings.
Many neurogenic and myopathic disorders can show these potentials.
They do not establish normal NMJ function.

options.text: A specific diagnostic marker of cataract
options.why: They are muscle electrical findings.
They are abnormal spontaneous resting activity.

stem: Large long-duration polyphasic motor units with reduced recruitment suggest what process?

options.why: Surviving motor axons sprout to supply additional fibers, enlarging motor units. Giant units can take a long time to develop in chronic neuropathy or post-polio states.
Lens pathology does not alter motor unit morphology.
Motor unit waveforms do not reflect retinal angiogenesis.
Myopathies more often show small short-duration units with early recruitment, though overlap exists.
The pattern indicates chronic neurogenic remodeling rather than simply normal myelin.

stem: Which electrophysiologic pattern most supports LEMS over MG?

options.text: Only a low-frequency decrement with normal postexercise amplitude
options.why: This may occur in MG and is less specific for LEMS.

options.text: A decrement alone proves LEMS rather than MG
options.why: Low-frequency decrement can occur in MG; marked increment is the more useful presynaptic clue.
An NMJ disorder does not primarily destroy sensory axons.

options.text: A marked CMAP increment after exercise or high-frequency stimulation
options.why: Presynaptic calcium accumulation can transiently improve transmitter release in LEMS. MG more typically shows low-frequency decrement.
This assesses optic pathway conduction rather than NMJ facilitation.

stem: Which time course best fits classic monophasic GBS?

options.text: Only one second of weakness with complete immediate recovery
options.why: This is not the typical progressive neuropathic syndrome.

options.text: Only isolated visual blur over years
options.why: This does not describe acute polyradiculoneuropathy.

options.text: Steady worsening for six months before nadir
options.why: This is more consistent with a chronic neuropathy such as CIDP.

options.text: Progressive weakness reaching nadir within four weeks, followed by a plateau and recovery
options.why: GBS is acute. Recovery may take weeks to months, and residual pain, fatigue, weakness, or paresthesias can persist.

options.text: A decade of continuous disability without acute onset
options.why: This is not the classic GBS course.

stem: Which finding casts doubt on uncomplicated GBS and should prompt a search for an alternative diagnosis?

options.why: This can be a major GBS complication.
An antecedent infection is common.
These can occur in GBS.
These are core supportive GBS features.

options.text: A sharp truncal sensory level and marked persistent asymmetry
options.why: A sensory level suggests spinal cord disease, while marked persistent asymmetry, early persistent sphincter dysfunction, or substantial CSF leukocytosis are warning signs.

stem: A patient with acute neuropathic weakness also has severe abdominal pain and dark urine after a new medication. Which mimic should be considered?

options.why: Porphyria can cause an acute motor-predominant neuropathy with abdominal and autonomic symptoms. GBS mimics also include toxic, metabolic, infectious, and vasculitic neuropathies.
Glaucoma does not explain limb paralysis and abdominal pain.
This childhood retinal tumor is not the described systemic mimic.
Lens opacity is unrelated to this motor-autonomic syndrome.
Macular degeneration does not explain acute neuropathy with abdominal symptoms.

stem: Which CSF pattern is most characteristic of GBS?

options.why: This is not the characteristic CSF finding.

options.text: Hundreds of neutrophils with very low glucose as the typical finding
options.why: This suggests infection rather than classic GBS.
MOGAD is a CNS disorder.
Albuminocytologic dissociation supports GBS, although CSF can be normal early. Marked pleocytosis should trigger evaluation for infectious, malignant, or other causes.
AQP4 antibodies support NMOSD, not GBS.

stem: A patient thought to have GBS has CSF with 120 leukocytes/mm3. What is the best interpretation?

options.text: Reconsider the diagnosis and investigate alternatives
options.why: The lecture flags counts above 50/mm3 as a warning. Mild pleocytosis can occur, but substantial leukocytosis raises concern for infection or another inflammatory process.

options.text: This is required for definite GBS
options.why: GBS typically shows few cells despite elevated protein.
Pleocytosis can be an infectious clue.
The atypical result warrants reassessment.
CIDP also generally has albuminocytologic dissociation, not marked leukocytosis.

stem: A patient has classic early GBS but nearly normal initial NCS. What is the best next interpretation?

options.text: Normal initial NCS definitively excludes GBS
options.why: Electrodiagnostic sensitivity depends on timing and pattern.

options.text: The patient must have a cataract
options.why: Lens disease does not explain acute areflexic weakness.

options.text: Begin chronic CIDP labeling solely because the first NCS is normal
options.why: Time course and repeat assessment are needed.

options.text: Early studies can be nondiagnostic; repeat electrophysiology if needed
options.why: Proximal/root abnormalities and evolving disease may not be obvious initially. F-wave changes can be informative; a normal early study does not safely exclude GBS.

options.text: Only sensory retinal testing can confirm GBS
options.why: GBS is a peripheral nerve/root disorder.

stem: A patient has ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, and areflexia after infection. Which GBS-spectrum syndrome is most likely?

options.why: A median wrist lesion cannot explain the triad.
The acute ocular-ataxic triad is more specific for Miller Fisher syndrome.
The triad is classic for Miller Fisher syndrome, often associated with anti-GQ1b antibodies. Related Bickerstaff brainstem encephalitis can add impaired consciousness or hyperreflexia.
This does not cause areflexia or ophthalmoplegia.
ALS does not usually present with acute postinfectious ophthalmoplegia and ataxia.

stem: A patient with postinfectious ophthalmoplegia and ataxia also has impaired consciousness and brisk reflexes. Which related syndrome is favored?

options.why: A focal peripheral nerve lesion cannot produce this syndrome.
This does not explain acute brainstem signs and altered consciousness.
The acute encephalopathic ophthalmoplegic syndrome is different.
Lens opacity does not cause brainstem dysfunction.
Altered consciousness or hyperreflexia points toward the Bickerstaff end of the anti-GQ1b spectrum rather than isolated classic Miller Fisher syndrome.

stem: An acute pure motor neuropathy shows reversible nodal conduction failure without temporal dispersion or other demyelinating features. Which GBS subtype is favored?

options.why: AMSAN also involves sensory axons, which are spared in the stated pure motor syndrome.
AIDP typically has broader demyelinating features such as slowing, prolonged latencies, and dispersion.
MG is an NMJ disorder rather than a motor axonal neuropathy.
AMAN may show reversible conduction failure at nodes before axonal degeneration. Conduction block alone should not automatically be interpreted as demyelination.
MS is CNS disease and does not cause this peripheral nodal pattern.

stem: A patient with GBS has rapidly declining respiratory measurements and weak cough but normal oxygen saturation. What should guide management?

options.text: Urgent monitored assessment for impending ventilatory failure
options.why: Oxygen saturation can remain normal early in neuromuscular respiratory failure. Serial respiratory mechanics, bulbar function, cough, and clinical trajectory inform timely airway support.

options.text: Wait until respiratory arrest to intubate
options.why: Anticipatory care is essential.
The primary problem is neuromuscular weakness rather than bronchospasm.

options.text: Normal oxygen saturation excludes respiratory risk
options.why: Ventilatory weakness can precede hypoxemia.

options.text: Discharge because GBS never affects breathing
options.why: A substantial minority require ventilation.

stem: Which immunotherapy approach is supported for significant GBS?

options.text: Long-term oral azathioprine as the only acute rescue
options.why: Its delayed immunosuppressive action is not an established substitute for IVIg or PLEX in acute GBS.

options.text: Routine IVIg plus PLEX for every case because effects always add
options.why: Trials do not show routine added benefit, and PLEX can remove administered immunoglobulin.

options.text: Corticosteroids alone as the preferred proven therapy
options.why: Unlike CIDP, GBS has not shown benefit from corticosteroids as standard treatment.

options.text: No monitoring because immunotherapy immediately reverses paralysis
options.why: Recovery is variable and acute complications remain possible.

options.text: IVIg or plasma exchange, with no routine added benefit from combining both
options.why: Both hasten recovery and have similar efficacy in trials. Supportive respiratory, autonomic, pain, and rehabilitation care remains essential; corticosteroids alone are not effective GBS treatment.

stem: A recovered patient remains fatigued with neuropathic pain and paresthesias. Which interpretation is most accurate?

options.text: Residual fatigue alone proves recurrent active demyelination
options.why: Persistent symptoms can reflect incomplete recovery; a new relapse requires clinical reassessment rather than fatigue alone.

options.text: Residual symptoms prove all initial treatment was inappropriate
options.why: Incomplete recovery does not establish treatment failure or wrong diagnosis.

options.text: All patients regain normal function in one day
options.why: This is inconsistent with GBS recovery.
Pain can occur during and after GBS.

options.text: Residual symptoms are common after GBS
options.why: Recovery can be prolonged and incomplete despite treatment. Prognostic models use clinical strength and severity measures, but individual trajectories vary.

stem: Which statement about infection and vaccination best reflects the evidence emphasized in the lecture?

options.why: GBS following vaccination is rare and risk depends on vaccine and context.
Only a small fraction of infections lead to GBS.

options.text: All vaccines are permanently forbidden after any neuropathy
options.why: That is not a justified universal rule.

options.text: Influenza infection carries greater GBS risk than influenza vaccination; future vaccination requires individualized assessment
options.why: A history temporally related to a vaccine warrants review of timing and specific vaccine guidance. The slide's blanket instruction to never repeat vaccination is too broad.

options.text: Influenza infection has no association with GBS
options.why: The lecture emphasizes a larger infection-associated risk.

stem: A patient has four months of symmetric proximal and distal weakness, vibration loss, and areflexia. Acquired demyelination is demonstrated in multiple nerves. Which phenotype fits?

options.why: A symmetric motor-predominant acquired demyelinating neuropathy can occur without prominent sensory symptoms; IVIg is often favored over steroids.

options.text: Anti-MAG distal acquired demyelinating symmetric neuropathy
options.why: Distal sensory-predominant demyelination with IgM paraprotein and anti-MAG antibodies is a distinct paraproteinemic neuropathy and often treatment-refractory.
This is the classic sensorimotor phenotype. The lecture estimates roughly half of cases are typical; mimics must be excluded before assigning the diagnosis.
Antibodies to nodal/paranodal adhesion proteins define a distinct category, often with poor IVIg response and selected benefit from B-cell-directed therapy.
CISP can produce sensory ataxia from proximal root involvement despite normal routine distal NCS; SSEPs, CSF, and root MRI may help.

stem: A patient initially labeled GBS continues to deteriorate ten weeks after onset and then has another relapse. Which diagnosis must be reconsidered?

options.why: Antibodies to nodal/paranodal adhesion proteins define a distinct category, often with poor IVIg response and selected benefit from B-cell-directed therapy.
Acute-onset CIDP can initially resemble GBS. Deterioration beyond eight weeks and recurrent worsening warrant reconsideration of a chronic inflammatory course.
CISP can produce sensory ataxia from proximal root involvement despite normal routine distal NCS; SSEPs, CSF, and root MRI may help.
Symmetric proximal and distal weakness, large-fiber sensory loss, and areflexia with chronic acquired demyelination characterize typical CIDP.
Polyneuropathy with organomegaly, endocrinopathy, monoclonal plasma cell disorder, and skin changes should prompt a systemic plasma-cell disorder evaluation.

stem: A patient develops prominent sensory ataxia and reduced reflexes, with little weakness but acquired demyelinating abnormalities on NCS. Which phenotype fits?

options.why: CISP can produce sensory ataxia from proximal root involvement despite normal routine distal NCS; SSEPs, CSF, and root MRI may help.
Sensory CIDP is a sensory-predominant variant. Distal sensory neuropathy and central dorsal column disease remain important alternatives.

options.text: Anti-MAG distal acquired demyelinating symmetric neuropathy
options.why: Distal sensory-predominant demyelination with IgM paraprotein and anti-MAG antibodies is a distinct paraproteinemic neuropathy and often treatment-refractory.
Asymmetric pure motor named-nerve weakness with conduction block and preserved sensory studies favors MMN, generally treated with IVIg.
Polyneuropathy with organomegaly, endocrinopathy, monoclonal plasma cell disorder, and skin changes should prompt a systemic plasma-cell disorder evaluation.

stem: Severe sensory ataxia occurs despite normal routine distal NCS. SSEPs, elevated CSF protein, and lumbar root abnormalities support proximal sensory root disease. Which syndrome fits?

options.why: CIDP may initially mimic GBS; continued deterioration beyond eight weeks or repeated relapses after the acute phase prompts reassessment.
Symmetric proximal and distal weakness, large-fiber sensory loss, and areflexia with chronic acquired demyelination characterize typical CIDP.
CISP affects proximal sensory roots, so routine distal studies can be normal. It is generally discussed as a related immune sensory syndrome rather than automatically equivalent to typical CIDP.
Sensory-predominant symptoms, ataxia, and reduced reflexes can occur, with electrophysiologic evidence supporting peripheral demyelination.
Asymmetric pure motor named-nerve weakness with conduction block and preserved sensory studies favors MMN, generally treated with IVIg.

stem: A patient has symmetric proximal and distal weakness with acquired demyelinating studies but no important sensory symptoms. Which CIDP variant fits?

options.why: Antibodies to nodal/paranodal adhesion proteins define a distinct category, often with poor IVIg response and selected benefit from B-cell-directed therapy.
Sensory-predominant symptoms, ataxia, and reduced reflexes can occur, with electrophysiologic evidence supporting peripheral demyelination.
Motor CIDP is a symmetric motor-predominant phenotype. Immunoglobulin is often preferred because corticosteroids can worsen some motor-predominant cases.
CISP can produce sensory ataxia from proximal root involvement despite normal routine distal NCS; SSEPs, CSF, and root MRI may help.
Symmetric proximal and distal weakness, large-fiber sensory loss, and areflexia with chronic acquired demyelination characterize typical CIDP.

stem: A patient has asymmetric distal upper-limb weakness and numbness affecting multiple nerves, with acquired demyelination. Which CIDP phenotype is most likely?

options.why: Polyneuropathy with organomegaly, endocrinopathy, monoclonal plasma cell disorder, and skin changes should prompt a systemic plasma-cell disorder evaluation.
MADSAM includes both motor and sensory involvement. MMN is motor-only and therefore less suitable when objective sensory abnormalities are present.
CISP can produce sensory ataxia from proximal root involvement despite normal routine distal NCS; SSEPs, CSF, and root MRI may help.
A symmetric motor-predominant acquired demyelinating neuropathy can occur without prominent sensory symptoms; IVIg is often favored over steroids.
Symmetric proximal and distal weakness, large-fiber sensory loss, and areflexia with chronic acquired demyelination characterize typical CIDP.

stem: An older man has slowly progressive distal sensory ataxia and tremor, prolonged distal latencies, an IgM monoclonal protein, and anti-MAG antibodies. Which diagnosis fits?

options.why: Asymmetric pure motor named-nerve weakness with conduction block and preserved sensory studies favors MMN, generally treated with IVIg.
Asymmetric sensory and motor demyelinating deficits in multiple nerves, often upper-limb predominant, fit multifocal CIDP/Lewis-Sumner syndrome.

options.text: Anti-MAG distal acquired demyelinating symmetric neuropathy
options.why: Anti-MAG neuropathy is strongly associated with an IgM paraprotein and distal sensory-predominant demyelination. It often responds less well to typical CIDP therapies.
CISP can produce sensory ataxia from proximal root involvement despite normal routine distal NCS; SSEPs, CSF, and root MRI may help.
Polyneuropathy with organomegaly, endocrinopathy, monoclonal plasma cell disorder, and skin changes should prompt a systemic plasma-cell disorder evaluation.

stem: A patient has severe sensory ataxia, tremor, distal weakness, and neurofascin-155 IgG4 antibodies with poor IVIg response. Which category is most appropriate?

options.why: Polyneuropathy with organomegaly, endocrinopathy, monoclonal plasma cell disorder, and skin changes should prompt a systemic plasma-cell disorder evaluation.
A symmetric motor-predominant acquired demyelinating neuropathy can occur without prominent sensory symptoms; IVIg is often favored over steroids.
Sensory-predominant symptoms, ataxia, and reduced reflexes can occur, with electrophysiologic evidence supporting peripheral demyelination.
CISP can produce sensory ataxia from proximal root involvement despite normal routine distal NCS; SSEPs, CSF, and root MRI may help.
Nodal/paranodal antibody-defined disorders are now separated from conventional CIDP. Selected patients may respond to rituximab or other antibody-directed approaches.

stem: A demyelinating neuropathy is accompanied by organomegaly, skin changes, endocrinopathy, and a monoclonal plasma-cell disorder. Which diagnosis should be considered?

options.why: A symmetric motor-predominant acquired demyelinating neuropathy can occur without prominent sensory symptoms; IVIg is often favored over steroids.
Asymmetric sensory and motor demyelinating deficits in multiple nerves, often upper-limb predominant, fit multifocal CIDP/Lewis-Sumner syndrome.
The systemic cluster is characteristic of POEMS and should not be treated as routine CIDP without evaluating the plasma-cell disorder.
CIDP may initially mimic GBS; continued deterioration beyond eight weeks or repeated relapses after the acute phase prompts reassessment.
CISP can produce sensory ataxia from proximal root involvement despite normal routine distal NCS; SSEPs, CSF, and root MRI may help.

stem: Which evidence is most important before diagnosing CIDP?

options.why: Fatigue without objective compatible findings is not enough.

options.text: A compatible clinical course plus convincing acquired demyelinating electrodiagnostic findings
options.why: Multiple formal criteria exist, but clinical pattern and properly performed NCS are central. Modest CSF protein elevation alone is a common source of overdiagnosis.

options.text: A normal sensory examination proves CIDP in all cases
options.why: CIDP phenotypes vary, but a normal sensory exam does not itself establish a diagnosis.

options.text: Any mild CSF protein increase regardless of symptoms
options.why: This is nonspecific and insufficient.

options.text: A single slowed nerve across a common entrapment site
options.why: Entrapment alone does not establish generalized CIDP.

stem: A cold hand produces prolonged distal latencies and slowed conduction. What should be done before attributing this to CIDP?

options.why: Cold-induced slowing is a confounder.

options.text: Label block from an equivocal amplitude change without checking stimulation
options.why: Submaximal stimulation and other technical factors can falsely suggest block.
This can compound overdiagnosis.

options.text: Ignore all nerve conduction data forever
options.why: Technically adequate NCS remains essential.

options.text: Warm the limb and verify technical factors and accepted thresholds
options.why: Temperature, measurement error, amplitude-dependent slowing, entrapment, and diabetes can create misleading findings. The lecture warns against equivocal slowing and unsupported block calls.

stem: Which finding is an electrophysiologic pitfall rather than convincing standalone evidence for CIDP?

options.text: Slowing confined to a common compression site
options.why: Focal entrapment can slow conduction without generalized acquired demyelination. Markedly low amplitudes and cold limbs also complicate interpretation.

options.text: Marked nonuniform slowing in several non-entrapment segments
options.why: This can support acquired demyelination in an appropriate clinical context.

options.text: Multiple appropriately measured prolonged F-wave latencies
options.why: This may support proximal demyelinating abnormalities in context.

options.text: Convincing temporal dispersion in multiple nerves
options.why: This may support demyelination when technical criteria are satisfied.
This can support acquired nerve dysfunction when interpreted correctly.

stem: What does a sural-sparing pattern mean in an acquired inflammatory neuropathy evaluation?

options.text: Relative preservation of the sural sensory response despite abnormal upper-limb sensory responses
options.why: This pattern can support inflammatory demyelinating neuropathy, including GBS or CIDP, but is neither required nor independently diagnostic.

options.text: A completely normal study in all nerves
options.why: Sural sparing is a relative pattern of abnormal and preserved responses.

options.text: Proof of a neuromuscular junction disorder
options.why: The pattern involves sensory nerve responses rather than NMJ transmission.
The sural nerve is a peripheral leg sensory nerve.

options.text: Normal motor responses with absent sensation in every nerve
options.why: That is not the definition.

stem: Does a patient with typical clinical CIDP and convincing acquired demyelinating NCS always need nerve biopsy?

options.text: No; biopsy is reserved for selected uncertain or alternative diagnoses
options.why: Routine biopsy is not necessary when clinical and NCS evidence is convincing. Vasculitis or infiltrative disease may create a separate biopsy indication.

options.text: Yes, because NCS never detects demyelination
options.why: NCS is central to CIDP assessment.

options.text: A biopsy is mandatory because mild CSF protein elevation is diagnostic
options.why: Mild protein elevation is nonspecific and does not create a universal biopsy requirement.

options.text: Yes, before any treatment in every case
options.why: This adds unnecessary invasive testing to an otherwise supported diagnosis.

options.text: No tests are needed for any patient with fatigue
options.why: The question assumes objective compatible findings; fatigue alone is insufficient.

stem: Which treatment set is appropriate for typical CIDP?

options.why: Typical CIDP is immune-mediated and is not treated as a persistent bacterial nerve infection.

options.text: Immunoglobulin, corticosteroids, and selected plasma exchange
options.why: IVIg or subcutaneous immunoglobulin and corticosteroids are major therapies; PLEX is effective but long-term access/logistics can limit use. This differs from GBS, where steroids are not effective standard treatment.

options.text: Acetylcholinesterase inhibition as the sole disease-modifying treatment
options.why: This can improve MG transmission but does not treat CIDP demyelination.

options.text: Corticosteroids are ineffective in every CIDP phenotype because they fail in GBS
options.why: Treatment evidence differs between chronic CIDP and acute GBS; motor phenotypes require additional nuance.

options.text: All patients must take lifelong IVIg without reassessment
options.why: Some stable patients can reduce or discontinue treatment with monitoring.

stem: A stable patient has received maintenance IVIg for CIDP for years. Which approach is reasonable?

options.text: Periodically reassess disease activity and consider supervised dose reduction or withdrawal
options.why: Some patients can discontinue without relapse. The lecture's approximate rate is cohort-dependent and does not justify abrupt cessation in every patient.

options.text: Stop abruptly in every patient based on one statistic
options.why: Withdrawal should be individualized and monitored.

options.text: Never reassess because all patients are permanently IVIg-dependent
options.why: Dependence varies and overtreatment can occur.

options.text: Use a positive serum MOG test as the only withdrawal criterion
options.why: MOGAD testing does not determine CIDP IVIg dependence.

options.text: Use permanent high-dose steroids without safety review
options.why: Long-term steroid toxicity and ongoing disease activity require reassessment.

stem: Which target is a Schwann-cell paranodal protein associated with tremor, sensory ataxia, and frequent IVIg refractoriness?

options.why: CNTN1 is an axonal paranodal adhesion molecule; nephrotic syndrome has been reported.
NF186 is a nodal axonal isoform involved in sodium channel organization, rather than the specified glial paranodal target.
AQP4 is an astrocytic CNS water channel, not the Schwann paranodal protein.
NF155 is a glial paranodal adhesion protein. IgG4-associated disease can respond better to B-cell-directed treatment than IVIg in selected patients.
CASPR1 is an axonal paranodal protein; severe neuropathic pain is a described clue.

stem: Which antibody target is an axonal nodal neurofascin isoform involved in sodium channel clustering?

options.why: NF186 and NF140 are axonal nodal isoforms, unlike glial paranodal NF155. Nodal disorders can have motor, sensory, and cranial manifestations.
NF155 is the glial paranodal isoform.
MOG is an outer CNS myelin protein, not a peripheral nodal neurofascin isoform.
RB regulates the cell cycle, not nodal adhesion.
AQP4 is an astrocyte water channel.

stem: A patient has severe neuropathic pain, distal weakness, and an IVIg-refractory antibody-mediated paranodal disorder. Which target is highlighted by that painful phenotype?

options.why: This is associated with Graves disease and thyroid ophthalmopathy.
This does not identify the antibody-defined nodopathy.
Contactin-associated protein 1 is a paranodal axonal adhesion protein. Severe neuropathic pain is a notable reported feature; phenotype is suggestive rather than perfectly specific.
Crystallin aggregation causes cataracts rather than nodopathy.
This is a postsynaptic NMJ target and does not cause a sensory painful neuropathy.

stem: Sensory ataxia and motor weakness with nephrotic syndrome accompany an IgG4 paranodal antibody. Which target is a recognized association?

options.why: ABCD1 variants cause adrenoleukodystrophy.
BRAF is an oncogenic pathway component rather than a paranodal antibody target.

CNTN1 autoimmunity can be associated with motor-predominant neuropathy, ataxia, nephrotic syndrome, and IVIg resistance. NF140/186 disease can also have renal associations; the antibody assay resolves overlap.
This is a hereditary pressure-palsy mechanism, not an IgG4 autoimmune renal association.
GALC deficiency causes Krabbe disease.

stem: A 34-year-old woman presents with palpitations, heat intolerance, and six months of increasing eye prominence. She reports gritty eyes on waking and cannot fully close her eyelids during sleep. Examination shows bilateral proptosis and restricted eye movements. Thyroid testing demonstrates suppressed TSH and elevated free thyroxine. Imaging shows enlarged extraocular muscles and increased orbital soft tissue. The clinical photograph is shown. Which disorder best explains the eye findings and risk of exposure-related corneal injury?

options.why: Corneal inflammation or ulceration can produce pain, photophobia, and reduced vision; it does not account for posterior retinal or optic disc pathology.

Orbital inflammation, matrix deposition, fat expansion, and eventual extraocular muscle fibrosis explain Graves ophthalmopathy. Incomplete lid closure exposes and dries the cornea; lubrication and protection are important while severity-specific treatment is evaluated.
Neurosensory retina separates from RPE, often causing flashes, floaters, and a curtain-like field defect; this requires urgent retinal assessment.
Deep painful scleral inflammation differs anatomically from uveitis, lens opacity, and retinal disease.
This is a melanocytic uveal malignancy, commonly choroidal and pigmented, with a propensity for liver metastasis; it is distinct from childhood retinoblastoma.

stem: A 69-year-old man with diabetes and atopic dermatitis reports a year of worsening vision. Headlights produce glare, colors appear faded, and he needs more illumination to read. He has no eye pain, flashes, floaters, or curtain-like field defect. Years earlier he received prolonged oral prednisone for severe dermatitis. His fundus is difficult to visualize because of an opacity in the optical media, shown here. Which diagnosis best unifies the gradual symptoms, examination, and multiple risk factors?

options.why: A lens opacity explains painless blur, glare, poor night vision, and faded colors. Age, diabetes, corticosteroids, and atopic dermatitis are relevant risks. Galactosemia, Wilson disease, trauma, and radiation are additional lecture associations.
Choroidal neovascularization causes hemorrhage, exudation, and rapid central distortion; it does not cause primary lens opacity.
Separation of posterior vitreous cortex from retina causes new floaters or flashes and may cause a retinal tear; it is not itself neurosensory retinal separation from RPE.
This is a melanocytic uveal malignancy, commonly choroidal and pigmented, with a propensity for liver metastasis; it is distinct from childhood retinoblastoma.
An orbital lymphoid tumor can cause progressive proptosis; biopsy establishes the nature of the mass rather than thyroid tests alone.

stem: A 64-year-old woman comes for an examination because she has started bumping into furniture. She can still read the central letters on an eye chart. She denies pain, redness, or abrupt visual loss. Automated fields show bilateral peripheral defects; gonioscopy demonstrates open angles. The optic disc appearance is shown. Her mother lost vision late in life. Which diagnosis explains the preserved early central acuity despite progressive peripheral loss and the structural disc change?

options.why: Choroidal neovascularization causes hemorrhage, exudation, and rapid central distortion; it does not cause primary lens opacity.

Chronic glaucomatous ganglion cell and axon loss causes peripheral field defects and cupping. The angle remains open but aqueous outflow resistance is elevated; pressure reduction helps prevent further irreversible damage.

stem: A 79-year-old woman has gradually increasing difficulty reading and recognizing faces. She continues to navigate around the house using peripheral vision. She denies eye pain or a sudden curtain. Examination shows yellow-white macular deposits, patches of pigment alteration, and irregular islands of atrophy. No fresh blood or neovascular membrane is identified. She asks whether cataract surgery will correct the central blind spots. Which diagnosis best localizes the primary disease responsible for these findings?

options.why: Acute profound painless monocular loss with retinal whitening and a cherry-red fovea indicates arterial ischemia, not gradual macular degeneration.
Deep painful scleral inflammation differs anatomically from uveitis, lens opacity, and retinal disease.
Choroidal neovascularization causes hemorrhage, exudation, and rapid central distortion; it does not cause primary lens opacity.
A cataract is a lens opacity causing painless gradual blur, glare, and impaired night vision; it does not produce retinal neovascularization or disc swelling.

The macular deposits are drusen, and the atrophic changes involve RPE and associated photoreceptors. Cataract surgery cannot reverse established macular atrophy. Follow-up matters because dry disease can progress or become neovascular.

stem: An 83-year-old man previously monitored for drusen reports that lines on the doorframe became wavy over several days. A dark central spot now interferes with reading. Peripheral navigation remains possible, and there is no severe ocular pain. The fundus photograph shows yellow material and a hemorrhagic macular lesion. Angiographic testing demonstrates leakage from an abnormal vascular membrane. Which diagnosis explains the change from a slowly progressive disorder to rapid central visual deterioration?

options.why: Conversion to VEGF-driven choroidal neovascularization causes fluid and blood leakage at the macula. Early anti-VEGF treatment can limit damage, although established scar or atrophy may constrain recovery.
Corneal inflammation or ulceration can produce pain, photophobia, and reduced vision; it does not account for posterior retinal or optic disc pathology.
Separation of posterior vitreous cortex from retina causes new floaters or flashes and may cause a retinal tear; it is not itself neurosensory retinal separation from RPE.
A cataract is a lens opacity causing painless gradual blur, glare, and impaired night vision; it does not produce retinal neovascularization or disc swelling.
Drusen and RPE atrophy cause gradual central visual impairment without the leaking neovascular membrane of wet AMD.

stem: A 57-year-old man has a pigmented choroidal lesion discovered during a routine examination. Over several years the mass enlarges and breaks through Bruch membrane, detaching overlying retina. Biopsy shows atypical epithelioid and spindle melanocytic cells. Molecular testing identifies a G-protein pathway driver. He undergoes local radiotherapy and is advised to continue systemic surveillance despite stable ocular findings. Which diagnosis best explains the morphology, genetics, and concern for delayed hematogenous metastasis?

options.why: Uveal melanoma commonly arises in choroid, can grow through Bruch membrane, and often harbors GNAQ/GNA11 rather than characteristic cutaneous BRAF drivers. Liver metastasis is a major long-term risk.
Drusen and RPE atrophy cause gradual central visual impairment without the leaking neovascular membrane of wet AMD.
Inflammation causes photophobia, pain, and anterior chamber cells and flare; lens opacity and retinal deposits have different locations.
Neurosensory retina separates from RPE, often causing flashes, floaters, and a curtain-like field defect; this requires urgent retinal assessment.
Acute profound painless monocular loss with retinal whitening and a cherry-red fovea indicates arterial ischemia, not gradual macular degeneration.

stem: A 68-year-old man develops a shower of floaters and intermittent flashes in one eye. Earlier that morning he noticed only moving specks, but by evening a dark curtain extends from the periphery toward the center. Dilated examination identifies a retinal break and the elevated folded tissue pictured. The ophthalmologist explains that an age-related vitreous separation likely exerted traction and created the break. Which current diagnosis best explains the curtain and requires time-sensitive retinal repair?

options.why: An orbital lymphoid tumor can cause progressive proptosis; biopsy establishes the nature of the mass rather than thyroid tests alone.
Choroidal neovascularization causes hemorrhage, exudation, and rapid central distortion; it does not cause primary lens opacity.

The curtain and detached folded neural retina indicate retinal detachment complicating PVD. A tear permits vitreous fluid under the retina in rhegmatogenous detachment; photoreceptor degeneration makes repair urgent.

stem: A 52-year-old with longstanding poorly controlled diabetes missed several retinal screening visits. He now has sudden painless visual obscuration after months of intermittent floaters. Fundus examination reveals abnormal new vessels at the disc and elsewhere, and ultrasound confirms vitreous hemorrhage. Fibrovascular tissue is exerting traction on the retina. Which stage of diabetic eye disease accounts for the fragile vessels and the risk of tractional detachment, rather than simply capillary microaneurysms?

options.why: Arteriolar sclerosis, copper or silver wiring, and AV nicking reflect chronic blood pressure injury; these are not lens changes.

stem: A 36-year-old woman reports weeks of headache that worsens when lying down, pulsatile tinnitus, and brief episodes of dimmed vision. Her corrected visual acuity is initially close to normal. The fundus photograph shows a swollen hyperemic optic disc with indistinct margins, and the other eye has a similar finding. The clinician arranges urgent evaluation of intracranial pressure and its cause before deciding whether lumbar puncture is appropriate. What is the specific term for this pressure-related disc appearance?

options.why: Papilledema is disc swelling due to raised ICP. Preserved initial central acuity does not remove the urgency. Imaging and cause-directed management distinguish mass lesions, venous causes, and idiopathic intracranial hypertension.
An obstructed anterior chamber angle causes an acutely painful red eye with markedly increased pressure; it is not a painless retinal degeneration.
Deep painful scleral inflammation differs anatomically from uveitis, lens opacity, and retinal disease.
Choroidal neovascularization causes hemorrhage, exudation, and rapid central distortion; it does not cause primary lens opacity.
Neurosensory retina separates from RPE, often causing flashes, floaters, and a curtain-like field defect; this requires urgent retinal assessment.

stem: Parents bring a 19-month-old child because one eye appears white in flash photographs and has begun turning inward. Examination reveals the cream-colored retinal lesion pictured; imaging identifies intratumoral calcification. There is no known family history. Genetic counseling is arranged because the clinician explains that absence of affected relatives does not exclude a new germline tumor-predisposition variant. Which diagnosis best accounts for the child's age, leukocoria, strabismus, and calcified intraocular mass?

options.why: Separation of posterior vitreous cortex from retina causes new floaters or flashes and may cause a retinal tear; it is not itself neurosensory retinal separation from RPE.
An orbital lymphoid tumor can cause progressive proptosis; biopsy establishes the nature of the mass rather than thyroid tests alone.

Retinoblastoma can be sporadic or heritable, including de novo germline RB1 variants. Early intraocular treatment has a high cure rate; laterality and family history alone cannot establish whether a case is heritable.

stem: A 46-year-old woman has profound painful visual loss with little recovery after an earlier similar episode. She also recalls several days of otherwise unexplained hiccups and vomiting. The shown MRI includes posterior optic pathway and chiasmal enhancement. Spinal imaging subsequently identifies a long central cord lesion. Serum testing using a cell-based assay detects AQP4-IgG. Which disorder best explains the combination of optic nerve distribution, brainstem symptoms, and the antibody-defined mechanism of injury?

options.why: MOGAD can cause bilateral anterior optic neuritis, ADEM-like encephalopathy, conus myelitis, or cortical encephalitis; high-quality serum MOG-IgG testing is important.

Posterior optic nerve/chiasm disease, area postrema symptoms, and longitudinally extensive myelitis are characteristic NMOSD clues. AQP4 antibodies target astrocytes, and severe attacks can leave major residual disability.
ALS causes combined upper and lower motor neuron degeneration without a primary sensory neuropathy; conduction block favors a treatable motor neuropathy.
Severe shoulder pain followed by patchy weakness can involve several nerves without fitting a single brachial plexus segment.
MMN produces asymmetric pure motor weakness in named nerve distributions, conduction block, and no upper motor neuron signs; sensory loss argues against it.

stem: A 12-year-old develops painful loss of vision in both eyes after a respiratory illness. Both optic discs are swollen. MRI shows extensive anterior optic nerve signal and enhancement around the nerves, as illustrated. The chiasm is relatively spared. Serum AQP4-IgG is negative, but a high-titer cell-based MOG-IgG assay is positive. The child improves after prompt corticosteroid treatment, and a taper is planned to reduce early recrudescence. Which antibody-associated disorder best fits this pattern?

options.why: LEMS causes proximal weakness, autonomic symptoms, reduced reflexes, and facilitation with exercise from presynaptic calcium-channel antibodies.
ALS causes combined upper and lower motor neuron degeneration without a primary sensory neuropathy; conduction block favors a treatable motor neuropathy.
Young men may develop focal hand and forearm wasting that progresses for years and then plateaus, associated with flexion-related cervical cord changes.
MMN produces asymmetric pure motor weakness in named nerve distributions, conduction block, and no upper motor neuron signs; sensory loss argues against it.

Bilateral anterior optic neuritis with perineural enhancement and disc edema favors MOGAD. High-titer serum testing in this fitting phenotype is meaningful; low-titer results in inappropriate screening are less reliable.

stem: A 26-year-old develops pain on eye movement and reduced color saturation in one eye. The MRI shows a relatively short intraorbital optic nerve lesion. She later develops a separate brainstem syndrome, and brain imaging shows characteristic ovoid periventricular plaques. CSF-restricted oligoclonal bands persist. AQP4-IgG and MOG-IgG testing is negative. Which diagnosis is most consistent with the optic nerve pattern and the subsequent evidence of CNS disease in characteristic separate locations?

options.why: Typical unilateral short-segment optic neuritis can be part of MS. The later clinical event, characteristic MRI locations, and intrathecal synthesis support the diagnosis after exclusion of better explanations.
GBS usually produces acute progressive areflexic weakness reaching nadir within four weeks, often with autonomic or respiratory involvement; chronic progression suggests CIDP.
ADEM typically causes a monophasic multifocal demyelinating illness with encephalopathy, often after infection; repeated temporally separate attacks favor another disorder.
Hereditary length-dependent neuropathy commonly produces early onset, high arches, hammer toes, distal weakness, and family history.
Dorsal root ganglion disease causes non-length-dependent sensory loss, sensory ataxia, and pseudo-weakness improved by visual guidance; causes include Sjogren disease, cancer, and pyridoxine excess.

stem: A 39-year-old has a severe episode of bilateral leg weakness, urinary retention, and a sensory level. MRI demonstrates a long central cervical cord lesion, shown here. She previously had an episode of severe optic neuritis. Serum AQP4-IgG is positive. The clinician explains that disability often accumulates through attacks with incomplete recovery rather than a continuously progressive interattack course. Which diagnosis is favored?

options.why: ADEM typically causes a monophasic multifocal demyelinating illness with encephalopathy, often after infection; repeated temporally separate attacks favor another disorder.
LEMS causes proximal weakness, autonomic symptoms, reduced reflexes, and facilitation with exercise from presynaptic calcium-channel antibodies.
The extensive central cord lesion and severe optic neuritis with AQP4 positivity support NMOSD. Both prompt attack treatment and prevention of future attacks matter.
X-linked spinal bulbar muscular atrophy causes slow bulbar and proximal weakness, facial or tongue fasciculations, and androgen-insensitivity signs such as gynecomastia.
Severe shoulder pain followed by patchy weakness can involve several nerves without fitting a single brachial plexus segment.

stem: A 20-year-old develops leg weakness, saddle sensory symptoms, and urinary retention. MRI shows long-segment lower cord and conus involvement with central gray matter signal. MOG-IgG is strongly positive by a cell-based serum assay. After acute therapy the patient regains strength but continues to have bladder dysfunction. Which diagnosis best explains the imaging distribution and the disparity between motor and sphincter recovery?

options.why: Conus involvement and gray-matter-predominant myelitis are MOGAD clues. Persistent sphincter or sexual dysfunction can remain despite good motor recovery.
GBS usually produces acute progressive areflexic weakness reaching nadir within four weeks, often with autonomic or respiratory involvement; chronic progression suggests CIDP.
MMN produces asymmetric pure motor weakness in named nerve distributions, conduction block, and no upper motor neuron signs; sensory loss argues against it.
Subacute memory, psychiatric, and seizure symptoms with supportive CNS inflammation suggest limbic encephalitis after exclusion of infectious and other causes.
Young men may develop focal hand and forearm wasting that progresses for years and then plateaus, associated with flexion-related cervical cord changes.

stem: A 31-year-old woman has a prior episode of internuclear ophthalmoplegia and now develops partial sensory symptoms in one leg. Cord MRI shows several short, predominantly peripheral lesions rather than one centrally extensive lesion. Brain imaging reveals periventricular and juxtacortical plaques. CSF-restricted bands are present. Which disorder best matches the combined distribution and temporally separated clinical episodes?

options.why: ALS causes combined upper and lower motor neuron degeneration without a primary sensory neuropathy; conduction block favors a treatable motor neuropathy.
Subacute memory, psychiatric, and seizure symptoms with supportive CNS inflammation suggest limbic encephalitis after exclusion of infectious and other causes.

options.text: Hereditary neuropathy with liability to pressure palsies
options.why: PMP22 deletion predisposes to recurrent focal neuropathies at pressure sites and multifocal demyelinating findings.

Short peripheral cord lesions with characteristic brain lesions and separate attacks fit MS better than classic extensive central NMOSD myelitis. The MRI pattern alone is not an absolute discriminator.
Young men may develop focal hand and forearm wasting that progresses for years and then plateaus, associated with flexion-related cervical cord changes.

stem: A patient with recurrent optic neuritis develops intractable vomiting and hiccups that do not respond to symptomatic medication. Abdominal evaluation is unrevealing. The shown brain MRI includes a dorsal medullary abnormality, and serum AQP4-IgG is positive. Which disease best explains why the gastrointestinal-type symptoms localize to a CNS region rather than the stomach?

options.why: MS causes CNS demyelinating lesions disseminated in space and time, commonly with persistent CSF-restricted oligoclonal bands; long central cord lesions or area postrema syndrome suggest alternatives.
MG causes fatigable ocular or bulbar weakness from postsynaptic NMJ autoimmunity; sensation and pupils are usually spared.
The area postrema in the dorsal medulla controls emetic responses and is a characteristic AQP4-NMOSD site. Its inflammation can cause persistent vomiting and hiccups.
LEMS causes proximal weakness, autonomic symptoms, reduced reflexes, and facilitation with exercise from presynaptic calcium-channel antibodies.
MOGAD can cause bilateral anterior optic neuritis, ADEM-like encephalopathy, conus myelitis, or cortical encephalitis; high-quality serum MOG-IgG testing is important.

stem: A 15-year-old presents with seizures, headache, and altered mental status. MRI shows cortical FLAIR hyperintensity with associated subcortical involvement, as illustrated. Infectious studies are unrevealing, and serum testing detects high-titer MOG-IgG in a compatible clinical setting. Which disorder can account for this cortical encephalitis phenotype in addition to its more familiar optic neuritis and myelitis presentations?

options.why: Severe shoulder pain followed by patchy weakness can involve several nerves without fitting a single brachial plexus segment.

options.text: Hereditary neuropathy with liability to pressure palsies
options.why: PMP22 deletion predisposes to recurrent focal neuropathies at pressure sites and multifocal demyelinating findings.
AQP4-NMOSD is an astrocytopathy associated with severe optic neuritis, longitudinally extensive myelitis, and area postrema syndrome; AQP4-IgG is a key biomarker.
Subacute memory, psychiatric, and seizure symptoms with supportive CNS inflammation suggest limbic encephalitis after exclusion of infectious and other causes.
MOGAD includes cortical encephalitis with seizures as well as optic neuritis, myelitis, and ADEM. Encephalopathy and cortical lesions should not automatically be forced into an MS diagnosis.

stem: A 28-year-old has two neurologic attacks separated by a year. The brain MRI shows small ovoid plaques in periventricular and other characteristic locations, as illustrated. Some lesions enhance while others do not. Susceptibility imaging reveals a central vein within several plaques. No infectious, vascular, or antibody-associated alternative better explains the presentation. Which diagnosis best combines the clinical course and imaging pattern?

options.why: MOGAD can cause bilateral anterior optic neuritis, ADEM-like encephalopathy, conus myelitis, or cortical encephalitis; high-quality serum MOG-IgG testing is important.

Characteristic lesion distribution, temporal heterogeneity, and perivenular imaging support MS in a fitting syndrome. The central vein sign adds specificity but does not independently replace all diagnostic judgment.
MG causes fatigable ocular or bulbar weakness from postsynaptic NMJ autoimmunity; sensation and pupils are usually spared.
LEMS causes proximal weakness, autonomic symptoms, reduced reflexes, and facilitation with exercise from presynaptic calcium-channel antibodies.
Subacute memory, psychiatric, and seizure symptoms with supportive CNS inflammation suggest limbic encephalitis after exclusion of infectious and other causes.

stem: What feature is demonstrated by the small central lines and dots within these plaques?

options.why: This is measured electrophysiologically in nerves.
These are microscopic retinal tumor arrangements, not brain MRI veins.
This is a fundoscopic optic nerve head finding.
The hypointense venous structure traverses the plaque and reflects perivenular inflammation. Appropriate acquisition, lesion selection, and defined thresholds matter.

stem: Which approximate normal lower-limb motor conduction velocity threshold is used in the lecture table?

options.why: This is not a physiologic routine motor NCS value.
This is far below usual healthy large-fiber motor conduction speed.

options.text: Any value is normal if amplitude is normal
options.why: Myelin dysfunction can slow conduction despite preserved amplitude.
The lecture table uses leg velocity above 40 m/s and arm above 45 m/s as broad teaching values. Actual interpretation uses nerve-, age-, height-, and temperature-specific laboratory norms.
NCS estimates segmental conduction speed.

stem: In the historical EFNS/PNS table shown in the lecture, which finding is a demyelinating motor criterion when present in the required number of nerves?

options.text: Only sensory symptoms without objective findings
options.why: Symptoms alone do not satisfy motor electrodiagnostic criteria.

options.text: Normal F waves and normal velocity in every nerve
options.why: These do not establish demyelination.

options.text: Distal motor latency at least 50% above the upper limit of normal
options.why: The lecture table includes substantial latency prolongation, velocity reduction, F-wave abnormalities, block, and dispersion with nerve-count and amplitude qualifications. Modern interpretation uses the full applicable criteria rather than one isolated number.

options.text: An isolated low CMAP amplitude with normal conduction speed
options.why: This favors axonal loss rather than establishing motor demyelination by itself.

options.text: A 1% latency increase in one cold nerve
options.why: This is not sufficient and may be technical variation.

stem: The historical criteria table lists conduction velocity at least 30% below the lower limit of normal. How should that threshold be used?

options.text: As a threshold applicable only to sensory loss without weakness
options.why: These are motor nerve criteria and must be interpreted within the whole clinical phenotype.

options.text: As a measure of visual acuity
options.why: Conduction velocity is a peripheral electrophysiologic variable.

options.text: With required nerve counts, technical adequacy, and other clinical/electrodiagnostic qualifications
options.why: The table is a historical teaching framework, not permission to diagnose CIDP from slight slowing or one entrapment segment. Thresholds must be applied in full.

options.text: As proof of CIDP from any single uncorrected measurement
options.why: A single value can be confounded and does not establish a disease.

options.text: As a rule that amplitudes and temperature never matter
options.why: Both affect interpretation.

stem: A patient with a demyelinating neuropathy has a monoclonal protein. Which approach is appropriate?

options.text: Assume the neuropathy is inflammatory solely because CSF protein is mildly high
options.why: Nonspecific protein elevation cannot substitute for evaluation of the paraprotein and the clinical phenotype.
MGUS and other nonmyeloma disorders also occur.
These are key POEMS clues.

options.text: Evaluate the plasma-cell disorder and systemic clues before labeling uncomplicated CIDP
options.why: Consider anti-MAG disease, POEMS, malignancy, and MGUS in clinical context. A paraprotein can be relevant even when the neuropathy resembles CIDP.
Some indicate a disease-driving or malignant process.
